Rules for Shibuya on Halloween Weekend

Shibuya’s government-enforced initiative to combat Halloween disturbances started in 2019, and rules have gotten stricter by the year in the hopes of combating violence, vandalism, littering and other reported disturbances in the area.

The key rules and restrictions in place for October 30 and November 1 include 24/7 littering patrol teams supported by designated garbage stations, prohibition of obstructive photography such as in the middle of crosswalks and narrow alleys that could block traffic, closure of all three major public smoking areas, barriers around the Hachiko statue and temporary suspension of alcohol sales from surrounding restaurants and retailers to nail down on Shibuya’s year-round ban on public street drinking after 6:00 p.m.

Halloween rules are not just limited to Shibuya. Celebrating Halloween in Tokyo should be a fun experience, but knowing the local guidelines and etiquette ensures the fun extends to everyone. Here are some tips and recommendations to keep in mind.

For your standard pre-packaged costumes of popular characters and go-to Halloween classics, Don Quijote and Village Vanguard are your best bet. These chains are all over Tokyo and are one-stop shops for everything you need from ready-to-wear costumes, wigs, masks, makeup and props.

If you’re going for a more elevated, cosplay-level look but either don’t know how to sew or ran out of time this year, you can turn to Nakano Broadway’s Mandarake Cos-Play kan. The building has several stores, each specializing in its own subsection of otaku culture. Cos-Play kan is overflowing with mannequins with costumes of iconic anime, comic book and game characters.

Cospatio is located in Akihabara’s Onoden building, and has an impressive lineup of costumes displayed with pictures of the corresponding characters. Some of the more premium costumes require a pre-order form, but Cospatio has plenty of ready-made cosplays along with wigs and accessories to complete the full look.

If you just need small touches to a costume or want to keep it simple, don’t skip the humble 100-yen shops. Shops like Daiso, Seria and Can Do have many cute festive headbands, hats, masks, wands, fake blood and even tiny costumes for your pets.
Cosplay Etiquette and How To Ask For A Photo
If you’re heading out in your costume, the best course of action is to simply be mindful of others.

Avoid realistic-looking weapon props, overly-revealing costumes and scary makeup or masks. These can scare children and may lead to questioning by police or denial of entry into public venues. Either cover up your costume or get dressed up at the venue. Cosplay events will usually have their own designated changing facilities to avoid disturbances. Do not use public restrooms inside train stations and convenience stores to change.

Like in any place and time, taking photos of cosplayers requires consent and mutual respect. Never snap sneaky or candid photos from a distance. Approach respectfully and ask before taking out your camera. Official events often have designated photography zones and require both cosplayers and photographers to carry participation certificates.
You can politely ask for a photo by saying “shashin yoroshii deshou ka?” (“Is it alright to take a photo?”) or more simply, “shashin ii desu ka?” while gesturing toward your camera.
To ask if it’s okay to upload their photo online, you can say, “SNS ni nosete mo ii desu ka?” (“Is posting on social media also ok?”)
